summary: RTP is used in many application areas and environments, which require different security mechanisms for confidentiality, integrity, and source authentication of RTP and RTCP packets. This informational document describes the available options.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC compares ways to protect RTP and RTCP traffic in different kinds of sessions. It helps application designers choose based on who needs protection, who holds the keys, and which devices handle the media.

questions: what is the difference between dtls-srtp and sdes
subtitle: A survey of RTP security mechanisms and the application requirements that guide their choice.

tldr.problem: RTP is used in different session topologies and application environments, so one security mechanism cannot meet every need. Developers may find it difficult to compare the available choices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys RTP topologies, packet protection, key-management approaches, and requirements such as confidentiality, integrity, source authentication, privacy, and interoperability.
tldr.outcome: It gives non-normative guidance and examples for choosing a mechanism. It does not prescribe one solution for every RTP application.

facts.label: Default SRTP transform
facts.value: AES Counter Mode with 128-bit keys and HMAC-SHA-1 with an 80-bit tag

facts.label: Unencrypted RTCP header
facts.value: First 8 bytes of the first RTCP packet header in each compound packet

facts.label: DTLS-SRTP handshake
facts.value: Two round trips without losses; one with TLS resumption

facts.label: Legacy RTP confidentiality
facts.value: DES or 3DES; not to be used

today: RFC 7201 is an Informational RFC published in April 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC notes that its survey is not exhaustive because new mechanisms are defined regularly.

sections.title: Session Topology Changes the Security Needs
sections.content:
RTP carries media in settings ranging from point-to-point calls to conferences, multicast, and streaming. The RFC says the range of applications and signaling methods has led to many security solutions, and its overview is not exhaustive or normative.

A mixer creates a new stream and must be trusted with the security context. A transport translator may relay packets without knowing that context, while a gateway or media transcoder may need access to it. In any-source multicast, every participant with the group key can decrypt and verify traffic, so the shared context cannot distinguish individual sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The path media takes affects who can read or change it. A device that mixes or converts media may need access to the keys, while a simple relay may not.

sections.title: Secure RTP and Key Management
sections.content:
Secure RTP (SRTP) can provide confidentiality, integrity, source authentication, and replay protection. It leaves RTP headers and the first 8 bytes of the first RTCP packet header in a compound packet unencrypted, while integrity-protecting the packets. SRTP has no built-in key-management solution and relies on an external protocol.

The RFC surveys DTLS-SRTP, MIKEY, SDP security descriptions, Encrypted Key Transport, and ZRTP. Their properties depend on the algorithms, key exchange, signaling, and trust placed in intermediaries. For example, security descriptions transport plaintext keys in SDP, while DTLS-SRTP establishes keys between peers and can bind the exchange to certificate fingerprints carried through signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: SRTP can protect media packets, but another method must establish and distribute the keys. The security achieved depends on that key method and on whether the people and systems involved can be trusted.

sections.title: Other Ways to Protect RTP
sections.content:
The RFC reviews several alternatives. Legacy RTP confidentiality based on DES or 3DES and plaintext keys in SDP has extremely weak security and is not to be used. IPsec can protect packets between network interfaces, but a tunnel that ends before the RTP endpoint can leave traffic exposed between the tunnel endpoint and the application.

RTP over TLS over TCP provides point-to-point security. DTLS can protect complete RTP packets over a datagram transport; unlike DTLS-SRTP, it encrypts the headers too. Media-content protection can encrypt the payload while leaving headers available to middleboxes, but may require a second security layer and separate key management.
sections.plainLanguage: Different mechanisms protect different parts of a media session. A tunnel may stop before the application, while content-only encryption leaves headers available for network devices to use.

sections.title: Questions for Application Designers
sections.content:
Designers should identify confidentiality goals, how long media must remain secret, possible information leaks from packet sizes or clear header extensions, and which devices can access keys or unencrypted media. They should decide whether integrity must be end-to-end or whether trusted middleboxes may modify media.

Source authentication depends on key management and on binding the media source to signaling or a verifiable identity. Privacy may require hiding peer addresses or changing stable RTCP CNAME values. The RFC recommends considering automatic key management, avoiding reuse of the same SRTP key and SSRC, preferring end-to-end security over tunnels where possible, and weighing interoperability against the risk of bid-down attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Before choosing a mechanism, decide who may see the media, who may change it, and how the receiver knows who sent it. Also consider what packet details can reveal and whether intermediaries can be trusted.

sections.title: Examples of Application Choices
sections.content:
The examples show different choices for SIP-established sessions, WebRTC, IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), 3GPP Packet-Switched Streaming Service, and RTSP 2.0. WebRTC requires SRTP with DTLS-SRTP keying. For SIP-established sessions, the RFC describes DTLS-SRTP with certificate fingerprints exchanged through signaling.

The other examples make different trust and interoperability choices. IMS uses security between endpoints and an access-edge node in many cases. The streaming example protects encoded media content but does not provide integrity checking for RTP headers. RTSP 2.0 uses SRTP with MIKEY keying and TLS-protected signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that browser media, telephone networks, and streaming systems can choose different ways to protect RTP. The right choice depends on each system's topology, trust relationships, and security goals.
